Sample: 400 U.S. adults (200 per group) recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity. Recruitment cost €2,000.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) for each group. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B (difference ≥ 1.5 points).; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A (difference ≥ 1.5 points).. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, no further investment is recommended.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Segmented Pilot Test: Residential vs Small Business" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct locations: a residential building (e.g., a multi‑family apartment complex) and a small gym or fitness center. In each location, place a compact self‑service unit at a visible, accessible spot. Track the following metrics: (1) trial adoption rate (number of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks); (2) purchase intent measured via a short survey asking about willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above comparable consumer units); and (3) wholesale sales data (if the unit is sold through a distributor, track units sold).. Sample: Residential pilot: 50 units placed in 10 buildings, targeting 2,000 residents. Small business pilot: 20 units placed in 10 gyms, targeting 2,000 gym members.. Measure: Trial adoption rate (percentage of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks) and purchase intent (percentage of surveyed residents or gym owners indicating intent to purchase at a premium price).. Predictions: T1: Residential pilot adoption rate ≥ 10% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed residents; small business pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed gym owners.; T2: Small business pilot adoption rate ≥ 15% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed gym owners; residential pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed residents.. Decision rule: If the residential pilot meets both adoption threshold (10%) and purchase intent threshold (20%), proceed to develop a differentiated residential proposition. If the small business pilot meets both thresholds, proceed to develop a differentiated small‑business proposition. If neither segment meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health benefits and taste) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium health and taste messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and sustainability as top reason in Premium Condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and premium health and taste as top reason in Sustainability Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score in the Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than in the Sustainability Condition, conclude that premium positioning drives higher demand. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude that sustainability messaging drives higher demand. If both conditions show similar intent, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Smart vs Premium Home Cook Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Smart Group (smart, subscription-based combi-steamer) or Premium Group (professional-grade, high-performance combi-steamer). Both groups see the same product description and price points.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks (estimated 250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy?"), WTP (percentage of price paid), and brand preference (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Smart Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Premium Group, indicating demand for subscription-based convenience.; T2: Premium Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Smart Group, indicating demand for professional-grade performance.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Sustainability Condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Commercial Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowner segment (T1) or a small business/commercial segment (T2). Each segment receives a product description of a consumer‑operated laundry solution with a price range of €800‑€1,200. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. Secondary questions assess willingness to pay a premium for durability and reliability.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 homeowners and 250 small businesses/commercial users, recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "yes" for each segment) and average maximum price paid.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay at least 15% more than small businesses for the same solution.; T2: Small businesses will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay at least 10% more than homeowners for the same solution.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for homeowners is at least 20 percentage points higher than for small businesses, proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If purchase intent for small businesses is at least 20 percentage points higher than for homeowners, proceed with a differentiated small‑business proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. Who benefits: Home barista enthusiasts who enjoy brewing espresso at home and value the ritual and taste of high-quality coffee.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from using a single consumer product to multiple specialized tools (e.g., espresso machine, grinder, filter) to achieve consistent, professional results, driven by the desire to elevate their coffee experience.. How value is captured: Simonelli Group can capture value by offering premium-priced, differentiated kits and accessories, and by leveraging its brand reputation for Italian craftsmanship to justify higher prices.. Assumptions: Home barista market is growing and willing to invest in specialized equipment.; Consumers differentiate between professional and consumer-grade products.; Simonelli can reach and serve this segment effectively.. Predictions: Surveyed home barista consumers will indicate intent to purchase multiple specialized tools rather than a single product.; Willingness to pay for premium features (e.g., compact design, integrated grinder) will be higher than for standard consumer machines.; Sales of differentiated kits will increase in regions where home barista culture is established..

T2: Simonelli Group will not develop a differentiated consumer proposition because the home barista market is small and unprofitable, and the company prioritizes its professional and commercial segments. Why behaviour changes: The company lacks evidence of sufficient consumer demand to justify investment in a new product line, and its resources are already allocated to higher-margin professional segments.. How value is captured: Value is captured through continued sales of existing professional and commercial products, which generate higher margins and are less sensitive to market fluctuations.. Assumptions: Home barista market size is insufficient to support a differentiated consumer proposition.; Simonelli's current professional line is already optimized for the target market.; The company has limited capacity to develop and market a new consumer product.. Predictions: Simonelli's revenue from professional and commercial segments will continue to grow or stabilize in the near term.; Consumer product sales will remain low or flat, indicating limited demand.; The company's financial performance will not be significantly impacted by a new consumer proposition..

Test "Consumer Intent Survey for Home Barista Segment" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with targeted recruitment of home barista enthusiasts (self-identified coffee drinkers who brew espresso at home). Participants complete a structured questionnaire measuring intent to purchase, willingness to pay, and current ownership of coffee equipment.. Sample: 300 respondents, recruited via social media and coffee forums, stratified by region to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Primary measure: percentage of respondents indicating "high" intent to purchase a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., espresso machine, grinder, or kit). Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (in euros) for the proposed product.. Predictions: T1: At least 40% of respondents will report high intent to purchase a differentiated consumer proposition, and the average willingness to pay will be above €200.; T2: Fewer than 30% of respondents will report high intent, and the average willingness to pay will be below €150.. Decision rule: If the observed intent rate is below 30%, conclude that the home barista market is too small to justify investment (support T2). If the intent rate is at least 40% and the average willingness to pay is above €200, conclude that a differentiated consumer proposition is viable (support T1). If the intent rate is between 30% and 40%, conduct a follow-up survey to validate willingness to pay and consider a limited launch.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging its Italian brand and existing professional reputation. The evidence shows a domestic flagship machine and a planned compact grinder, but consumer demand remains unproven. A limited pilot test (e.g., a 6‑week online survey with 300 respondents) is recommended to validate intent and willingness to pay. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging its Italian brand and existing professional reputation. The evidence shows a domestic flagship machine and a planned compact grinder, but consumer demand remains unproven. A limited pilot test (e.g., a 6‑week online survey with 300 respondents) is recommended to validate intent and willingness to pay. Target customer: Home barista enthusiasts who brew espresso at home and value quality, convenience, and the ritual of coffee preparation.. Value proposition: A premium, differentiated consumer kit (e.g., espresso machine, compact grinder, and complementary accessories) that offers consistent, professional results and aligns with the lifestyle of coffee aficionados.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Intent Survey for Home Barista Segment (300 respondents, €15,000, 6 weeks) to measure intent to purchase and willingness to pay.. Uncertainty: The size of the home barista market and Simonelli's consumer revenue are unknown from public sources. The survey results may not reflect actual purchase intent or willingness to pay.. Would change if: If the survey shows fewer than 30% of respondents report high intent to purchase, the recommendation would shift to maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion.; If the survey reveals a willingness to pay below €200, the investment case would weaken, suggesting the market is too small to justify a differentiated proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Home Barista Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 self-identified home baristas (regular home coffee preparation) and 150 non-home baristas (occasional home coffee). Recruited via coffee forums and social media.. Measure: 1) WTP for a machine described as emphasizing social interaction (T1). 2) WTP for a machine described as emphasizing convenience and ease of use (T2). 3) Binary choice: prefer social experience or convenience.. Predictions: T1: Home baristas will show higher WTP for the social experience description and choose social experience over convenience.; T2: Non-home baristas will show higher WTP for the convenience description and choose convenience over social experience.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the social experience description among home baristas is at least 10 percentage points higher than the average WTP for the convenience description, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the convenience description among non-home baristas is at least 10 percentage points higher than the average WTP for the social experience description, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the 10-point threshold, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes the social experience of home barista, leveraging community features and social marketing. Conduct a small-scale willingness-to-pay test to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes the social experience of home barista, leveraging community features and social marketing. Conduct a small-scale willingness-to-pay test to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Home baristas and coffee enthusiasts who value the social aspect of coffee culture.. Value proposition: A machine that creates a third-place experience, offering community features, social sharing, and a platform for connecting with other home baristas.. Favoured theory: T1. Test "Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of 500 home cooks (aged 25-55) who have purchased a kitchen appliance in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing convenience, recurring revenue, and smart home integration; Group B sees a premium, high-performance combi-steamer description emphasizing professional-grade cooking, superior results, and brand prestige. Both groups view a neutral product description and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a monthly subscription fee (or a premium price).. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.. Measure: Purchase intent (7-point scale) and willingness to pay (monthly subscription fee or premium price).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a subscription fee than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium price than Group A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Group A and Group B is at least 1.5 points (e.g., Group A = 5.5 and Group B = 4.0), we conclude that the subscription messaging (T1) is more effective. If the difference is at least 1.5 points in favor of the premium messaging (Group B = 5.5 and Group A = 4.0), we conclude that premium positioning (T2) is more effective. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude neither theory is significantly supported and recommend further market research.. Cost: 8000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed subscription vs premium messaging test (X1) to empirically compare home cook demand for a subscription-based smart combi-steamer versus a premium, high-performance model. If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in purchase intent in favor of subscription messaging, develop a differentiated subscription proposition; otherwise, maintain the premium positioning and consider additional market research. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-D) concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2. Therefore the theory remains unchanged. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Run the proposed subscription vs premium messaging test (X1) to empirically compare home cook demand for a subscription-based smart combi-steamer versus a premium, high-performance model. If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in purchase intent in favor of subscription messaging, develop a differentiated subscription proposition; otherwise, maintain the premium positioning and consider additional market research. Target customer: Home cooks who value convenience, recurring revenue, and smart home integration, as identified by the test.. Value proposition: A subscription-based smart combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, leveraging RATIONAL's existing B2B reputation to build trust.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

Test "Self-service vs machine choice test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: convenience condition (emphasizes time savings and self-service ease) or cost condition (emphasizes lower long-term ownership costs). They view a product description of a self-service unit and a comparable machine, and indicate which they would choose and the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (200 per condition).. Measure: Primary measure: choice of self-service unit vs machine. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay for the chosen option.. Predictions: T1: In the convenience condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the cost condition.; T2: In the cost condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the convenience condition.. Decision rule: If the difference in choice rates between the two conditions is at least 15 percentage points, we conclude that the corresponding theory is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported. If the difference is inconclusive, we recommend further testing.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Test "Home Barista Preference Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home barista demographics (self-identified coffee enthusiasts). They view two machine concepts: (A) a premium professional‑grade machine with advanced controls and a compact design, and (B) a convenience‑focused machine with simplified controls and a compact design. Participants rank the two machines on a 7‑point scale (1‑very important, 7‑not important) and indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. The survey also includes a brief demographic question to ensure representation.. Sample: 300 participants, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions to reflect home barista demographics. Recruitment through coffee forums, social media, and partner channels.. Measure: Primary measure: average ranking of the premium machine (T1) versus the convenience machine (T2) across participants. Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the premium machine.. Predictions: T1: Participants will rank the premium machine higher than the convenience machine and report higher willingness to pay for the premium machine.; T2: Participants will rank the convenience machine higher than the premium machine and report higher willingness to pay for the convenience machine.. Decision rule: If the average ranking of the premium machine is at least 1.5 points higher than the convenience machine and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for the premium professional use case. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on the existing professional line.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
